content: Coagulation necrosis is a pathological process characterized by hyper-eosinophilia and nuclear changes, including pyknosis (condensation of the nucleus), followed by karyorrhexis (fragmentation of the nucleus) and karyolysis (dissolution of the nucleus). This process ultimately results in the complete loss of nuclei and the disappearance of cytoplasmic cross-striations. These changes typically become visible within 4 to 12 hours following myocardial infarction, with the earliest signs often appearing closer to the 12-hour mark. Necrotic myocytes may retain their striations for an extended period. During this time, acute inflammation becomes evident, marked by neutrophilic infiltration, edema, and hemorrhage, which are also generally observed within the 4 to 12-hour window, again more prominently around 12 hours post-infarction. The interstitial space at the periphery of the infarcted area is initially infiltrated by neutrophils, which are later replaced by lymphocytes and macrophages. These macrophages play a critical role in phagocytosing or engulfing the debris of necrotic myocytes. As the necrotic area undergoes repair, it becomes surrounded and progressively invaded by granulation tissue. This granulation tissue eventually replaces the infarcted region with a fibrous or collagenous scar, a hallmark of the wound healing process. The interstitial space, or the extracellular space outside of blood vessels, may also become infiltrated with red blood cells during this phase. By approximately 3 to 10 days post-infarction, the periphery of the infarcted area begins to show infiltration by macrophages, lymphocytes, eosinophils, fibroblasts, and newly formed capillaries. This cellular infiltration is a key step in the repair and remodeling process. Contraction band necrosis, a distinct pathological feature, is characterized by hyper-eosinophilic transverse bands of precipitated myofibrils within dead myocytes. This phenomenon is typically observed at the edges of an infarct or in cases of reperfusion injury, such as those occurring after thrombolytic therapy.
